# New Physics Effects on Neutrino Oscillations and Long-Baseline Experiments

## Extra Matter Effects from Beyond-Standard-Model Physics

The Standard Model has proven remarkably successful in describing neutrino oscillation phenomena, yet it remains an incomplete theory, motivating searches for physics beyond its framework. One particularly interesting avenue for probing new physics arises from the possibility that additional interactions—not accounted for in the Standard Model—could introduce novel matter effects on neutrino propagation. Such effects would manifest whenever new physics couples differently to the three neutrino flavors (electron, muon, and tau), thereby breaking the flavor universality that would otherwise render these interactions invisible in oscillation experiments. When neutrinos propagate through matter, these flavor-dependent interactions modify the effective Hamiltonian governing oscillations, potentially producing observable deviations from Standard Model predictions in long-baseline neutrino experiments.

## Constraining New Matter Effects with Long-Baseline Experiments

Building on this theoretical motivation, prior work (Ref. 1) has proposed a concrete experimental strategy for constraining the magnitude of these hypothetical extra matter effects. Specifically, this approach leverages the high-energy neutrino beam produced by the Fermilab-NuMI beamline, directed toward the future Hyper-Kamiokande detector, currently in the planning stages. This long-baseline configuration is particularly well-suited to this task because the extended baseline allows matter effects to accumulate over a significant distance, while the high-energy beam provides access to oscillation phenomena at energies where new physics contributions might be most pronounced. By comparing observed oscillation patterns against Standard Model expectations, one can place quantitative bounds on the strength of any new flavor-dependent matter interactions.

A crucial caveat to this proposed constraint concerns the mixing angle θ₂₃, one of the fundamental parameters governing neutrino oscillations. The sensitivity of the Fermilab-NuMI–Hyper-Kamiokande setup to new matter effects depends critically on the vacuum value of sin²2θ₂₃ not lying too close to unity. This is because when sin²2θ₂₃ approaches its maximal value, the oscillation probabilities become less sensitive to small perturbations from new physics, effectively degrading the experiment's ability to disentangle genuine new-physics signals from Standard Model backgrounds. Understanding this dependence is essential for properly interpreting the constraints derivable from this experimental setup and for assessing how robust these bounds are given current uncertainties in θ₂₃.

## From Experimental Constraints to Model-Building Implications

The present talk extends this line of investigation by addressing a natural and important question: how can the experimental constraints on extra matter effects be translated into concrete limits on the parameters of specific new physics models? While the long-baseline experimental strategy provides bounds on an effective phenomenological parameter characterizing the extra matter effect, connecting this to actual particle physics models requires establishing a mapping between this effective parameter and the underlying coupling constants and mass scales that define a given theory. This translation is essential for assessing the true discovery potential and constraining power of the proposed experimental setup, as it allows theorists to determine whether realistic new physics scenarios could produce effects large enough to be detected, or conversely, whether a null result would meaningfully exclude regions of parameter space in specific models.

## Application to Topcolor Assisted Technicolor

As a concrete illustration of this general framework, the talk specifically examines topcolor assisted technicolor as an example model where the derived limits on couplings and masses would find direct application. Topcolor assisted technicolor represents a class of dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking models that combines technicolor interactions—responsible for breaking electroweak symmetry—with an additional topcolor interaction that generates the large mass of the top quark through new strong dynamics. Because such models naturally introduce new gauge bosons or other mediators that can couple differently to different fermion generations, they provide a well-motivated framework in which flavor-dependent neutrino matter effects could naturally arise. By working through the details of how the topcolor assisted technicolor framework generates extra matter effects for neutrinos, the talk demonstrates explicitly how the general experimental constraint on matter-effect magnitude can be reinterpreted as specific bounds on the coupling strengths and mass scales characterizing the new gauge interactions in this model. This exercise serves as a template for connecting phenomenological neutrino oscillation constraints to the parameter spaces of concrete beyond-Standard-Model theories, illustrating the broader utility of long-baseline neutrino experiments as probes of new physics beyond their traditional role in measuring standard oscillation parameters.

# Probing New Physics Through Flavor-Dependent Matter Effects in Long-Baseline Neutrino Oscillations

## Introduction

The discovery of neutrino oscillations has provided compelling evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model, establishing that neutrinos possess non-zero masses and that the three known flavors mix through the PMNS matrix. While the standard three-flavor oscillation framework, incorporating well-established MSW matter effects, has proven remarkably successful in describing data from solar, atmospheric, reactor, and accelerator-based experiments, it remains an open question whether additional new physics contributions might modify neutrino propagation through matter in ways that deviate from the Standard Model predictions with only weak charged and neutral current interactions.

## Motivation for Flavor-Dependent Non-Standard Matter Effects

Beyond the well-known coherent forward scattering effects that generate the standard MSW potential, several classes of new physics models predict additional non-standard interactions (NSI) between neutrinos and the fermions comprising ordinary matter. These non-standard matter effects, if they exist, would generically be flavor-dependent, meaning that they could affect electron, muon, and tau neutrinos differently as they propagate through the Earth. Such effects could arise from a variety of ultraviolet completions, including models with extra gauge bosons, leptoquarks, or extended Higgs sectors that couple to both neutrinos and Standard Model fermions in flavor non-universal ways.

Among the theoretically motivated scenarios capable of generating such effects are models based on topcolor assisted technicolor (TC2), which was originally proposed to explain the large mass of the top quark through a new strong dynamics coupling preferentially to third-generation fermions. In such frameworks, new heavy gauge bosons or scalar states can mediate additional neutrino-matter interactions with couplings and masses that are, in principle, free parameters constrained only by other phenomenological considerations. This makes long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments a potentially powerful and complementary probe of such new physics, since the matter effects accumulate coherently over the long propagation distances characteristic of these experiments, potentially amplifying otherwise minuscule new physics signals to observable levels.

## Experimental Setup: NuMI Beam to Hyper-Kamiokande

To investigate this possibility in a concrete and realistic experimental context, this work considers a proposed long-baseline configuration in which the existing Fermilab NuMI neutrino beam is redirected toward the planned Hyper-Kamiokande detector in Japan. This configuration would provide an exceptionally long baseline, traversing a substantial portion of the Earth's mantle, thereby maximizing the accumulated matter effect and enhancing sensitivity to any non-standard flavor-dependent interactions relative to shorter-baseline experiments such as T2K or the standard NuMI-to-Super-Kamiokande setup.

The high-intensity NuMI beam combined with the enormous fiducial volume and excellent particle identification capabilities of Hyper-Kamiokande would enable precision measurements of both muon neutrino disappearance and electron neutrino appearance channels over an extended range of neutrino energies. Crucially, the sensitivity of this experimental configuration to new matter effects depends sensitively on the true value of the atmospheric mixing angle θ₂₃, since the analysis in this work demonstrates that discriminating power for non-standard interactions is significantly degraded when sin²2θ₂₃ approaches unity—that is, when θ₂₃ lies close to maximal mixing. This dependence arises because certain oscillation channels that are particularly sensitive to non-standard matter effects become degenerate with standard oscillation parameters in the maximal mixing limit, complicating the extraction of new physics signals from the data.

## From Oscillation Constraints to Particle Physics Parameters

The central contribution of this work lies in establishing a direct and quantitative connection between the experimentally accessible constraints on non-standard matter effects—typically parametrized in terms of effective NSI parameters ε that modify the neutrino evolution Hamiltonian—and the fundamental coupling constants and mass scales of specific ultraviolet-complete new physics models. Rather than presenting constraints purely in the abstract language of effective field theory parameters, this analysis explicitly maps the projected sensitivity of the NuMI–Hyper-Kamiokande experiment onto the parameter space of topcolor assisted technicolor models, translating bounds on ε into limits on the masses of the new gauge bosons or scalars predicted by these models and their couplings to neutrinos and matter fermions.

This translation is performed by computing the effective four-fermion interactions induced by the exchange of the new heavy states predicted in the TC2 framework and matching these onto the standard NSI parametrization used in the oscillation analysis. The resulting exclusion contours in the coupling-versus-mass plane provide a direct assessment of the discovery or exclusion reach of the proposed experiment for this class of models, expressed in terms of physically meaningful and experimentally testable quantities.

## Conclusions and Outlook

This work demonstrates that a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment utilizing the Fermilab NuMI beam directed at Hyper-Kamiokande offers a promising avenue for probing new physics beyond the Standard Model through its sensitivity to flavor-dependent non-standard matter effects, provided that the true value of θ₂₃ deviates sufficiently from maximal mixing. By explicitly connecting the resulting constraints on non-standard interaction parameters to the coupling constants and mass scales of concrete new physics scenarios such as topcolor assisted technicolor, this analysis illustrates the broader utility of next-generation long-baseline neutrino facilities as tools not only for precision measurements of standard oscillation parameters but also for direct tests of specific, well-motivated extensions of the Standard Model. These results motivate further study of how the physics reach of proposed long-baseline experiments can be leveraged to constrain a wider array of new physics models through their imprint on neutrino propagation through matter.

# Beyond the Standard Model: The Search for New Physics

For nearly five decades, the Standard Model of particle physics has stood as one of humanity's most successful scientific achievements. This theoretical framework describes the fundamental particles that make up matter and the forces that govern their interactions—electromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear forces. With remarkable precision, it has predicted the existence of particles like the Higgs boson, discovered in 2012 at CERN, confirming decades of theoretical work.

Yet despite its successes, the Standard Model is widely acknowledged to be incomplete. It fails to account for several fundamental phenomena that we observe in the universe. Dark matter, which makes up roughly 27% of the universe's mass-energy content, has no place within the current framework. Dark energy, responsible for the accelerating expansion of the universe, remains equally mysterious. The model also cannot explain gravity within its quantum framework, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of how the four fundamental forces relate to one another.

These limitations have driven physicists to search for what many call "New Physics"—theoretical extensions or entirely new frameworks that could address these shortcomings. Various approaches have emerged over the years, including supersymmetry, which proposes that every particle has a yet-undiscovered partner particle, and string theory, which suggests that fundamental particles are actually vibrating strings existing in multiple dimensions.

Experimental facilities like the Large Hadron Collider continue to search for evidence of new particles or unexpected phenomena that might point toward physics beyond the Standard Model. Each experiment that confirms Standard Model predictions, while validating current theory, also somewhat frustrates physicists hoping to find cracks that would reveal new physics.

The tension between the Standard Model's proven accuracy and its acknowledged incompleteness represents one of the most compelling puzzles in modern science. Whether through the discovery of new particles, unexpected experimental anomalies, or breakthrough theoretical insights, the search continues for a more complete understanding of our universe—one that might finally unite our understanding of the quantum world with gravity, explain the true nature of dark matter and dark energy, and perhaps reveal an entirely new paradigm that will eventually succeed where the Standard Model, despite all its achievements, ultimately falls short.

# Abstract

Long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments provide a unique opportunity to probe physics beyond the Standard Model through non-standard interactions (NSI) in the neutrino sector, which can manifest as anomalous matter effects during propagation through Earth. In this talk, we explore the physics potential of directing the Fermilab-NuMI neutrino beam toward the Hyper-Kamiokande detector, exploiting the resulting long baseline (~2500 km) to enhance sensitivity to NSI parameters that modify the effective matter potential.

Building on a previous theoretical argument demonstrating that octant degeneracies in sin²2θ23 can serve as a sensitive probe of non-standard matter effects, we examine how the extended baseline and the well-characterized NuMI beam properties combine to sharpen this sensitivity substantially beyond current facilities such as T2K and NOvA, and complement upcoming DUNE measurements. We present quantitative sensitivity projections for diagonal and off-diagonal NSI parameters (particularly ε_ee, ε_μτ, and ε_ττ), showing how the interplay between matter-enhanced oscillation probabilities and the octant ambiguity in θ23 can either mimic or reveal genuine new physics signals.

Using realistic beam flux simulations, detector response models for Hyper-Kamiokande, and statistical treatments of systematic uncertainties, we quantify the expected exclusion limits and discovery reach for NSI couplings as a function of exposure and beam configuration. We further discuss the complementarity between this NuMI–Hyper-K configuration and existing/proposed experiments, highlighting scenarios where degeneracies between standard oscillation parameters and NSI effects could be resolved through combined baseline and detector technology diversity. Our results indicate that this configuration offers a compelling opportunity to either significantly constrain NSI parameter space or provide corroborating evidence for anomalies suggested by current data, positioning it as a valuable complement to the global long-baseline neutrino program in the search for new physics in the neutrino sector.

# Neutrino Oscillations as a Window on New Physics: From Long-Baseline Experiments to Topcolor Assisted Technicolor

## Summary

Long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments—DUNE, T2HK, NOvA—are typically framed as precision tools for measuring standard three-flavor parameters: mixing angles, the CP-violating phase δ, and the mass ordering. This talk explores a complementary role: these facilities as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model, with a particular focus on how they constrain strongly-coupled electroweak symmetry breaking scenarios like Topcolor Assisted Technicolor (TC2).

**The connection is indirect but powerful.** TC2 and related dynamical EWSB models generically predict:

- **Extended scalar/pseudoscalar sectors** (top-pions, top-Higgs states) that couple preferentially to third-generation fermions
- **New heavy gauge bosons** (colorons, Z') from the extended color and hypercharge symmetries
- **Modified Yukawa structures**, since technicolor dynamics generates fermion masses without a fundamental Higgs, requiring extended interactions to explain the top quark's large mass

These new states can feed into the neutrino sector in several ways:

1. **Non-standard interactions (NSIs):** Heavy Z'-like states from extended color/technicolor sectors can induce four-fermion operators affecting neutrino production, propagation, and detection. Matter NSI parameters (ε_αβ) shift the effective Hamiltonian governing oscillations, mimicking or masking CP violation and mass-ordering signals.

2. **Radiative corrections to neutrino mass generation:** If TC2-type dynamics contributes to seesaw-like mechanisms (via new scalars coupling to right-handed neutrinos), the resulting mass matrix textures leave imprints on mixing angle correlations testable at DUNE's precision level.

3. **Long-range interactions from light pseudo-Goldstone bosons:** Some technicolor-inspired models predict light scalars whose exchange generates energy-dependent matter effects distinguishable from standard MSW physics over ~1000 km baselines.

**Why long-baseline experiments matter here:** The extended matter path length and broad-band beam energy coverage (DUNE: 0.5–5 GeV over 1300 km) provide sensitivity to subtle energy-dependent deviations from standard oscillation probability formulas—precisely the signature of NSI-type operators from new heavy mediators. Combined near/far detector designs allow separation of production/detection NSI effects from genuine propagation effects.

**Outlook:** While DUNE and Hyper-K were not designed with TC2 in mind, global fits incorporating NSI parameters alongside standard oscillation parameters can set complementary bounds on the flavor structure of new physics—bounds that intersect meaningfully with collider constraints on colorons and top-pions from the LHC. This synergy exemplifies how "precision" neutrino physics extends its reach into the broader landscape of strongly-coupled BSM model building.

# Abstract

Neutrino oscillation experiments provide a sensitive probe of new physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly through matter effects arising from novel flavor-dependent interactions. In this work, we investigate how the NuMI beam, when detected by the upcoming Hyper-Kamiokande experiment, can constrain new physics scenarios involving flavor-dependent long-range or matter-induced forces mediated by light new particles coupling to Standard Model fermions. The long baseline and off-axis configuration of NuMI-Hyper-K, combined with the passage of neutrinos through the Earth's crust and mantle, make this setup particularly sensitive to non-standard matter potentials that modify the effective Hamiltonian governing neutrino flavor evolution.

We systematically explore how new interactions—parametrized either as effective four-fermion operators or as mediated by a new gauge boson with mass $m_{Z'}$ and coupling $g'$ to combinations of lepton and quark flavor currents—induce shifts in the oscillation probabilities relevant to both appearance ($\nu_\mu \to \nu_e$) and disappearance ($\nu_\mu \to \nu_\mu$) channels. These new matter effects can mimic or degenerate with standard oscillation parameters, including the mass ordering and the CP-violating phase $\delta_{CP}$, motivating a careful global analysis to disentangle new physics contributions from the standard three-flavor oscillation framework.

Using realistic estimates of the NuMI flux at the Hyper-Kamiokande site, expected backgrounds, and systematic uncertainties, we perform a statistical analysis to derive projected sensitivities on the new coupling $g'$ as a function of the mediator mass $m_{Z'}$, spanning the sub-GeV to multi-GeV mass range relevant to light $Z'$ models such as those associated with gauged $L_\mu - L_\tau$ or other flavor-specific symmetries. We find that NuMI-Hyper-K can improve upon existing long-range force and non-standard interaction (NSI) constraints in specific regions of parameter space, particularly for mediator masses below the MeV--GeV scale, where oscillation-based probes are complementary to laboratory and astrophysical bounds. We further discuss how the resulting limits translate into constraints on the new particle's coupling to first-generation quarks and leptons, providing a benchmark for how next-generation oscillation facilities can serve as a discovery or exclusion tool for physics beyond the Standard Model in the neutrino sector.

# Constraining Nonstandard Neutrino Interactions at a Fermilab-to-Hyper-Kamiokande Baseline

## Abstract Summary

We present a technical analysis of the sensitivity of a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment, utilizing a high-intensity neutrino beam from Fermilab directed toward a next-generation Hyper-Kamiokande-class detector, to nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSI). Building on our earlier work [Ref. 1], we extend the phenomenological framework to explore how new physics scenarios—particularly those motivated by topcolor-assisted technicolor models—can be probed through subdominant matter effects in long-baseline oscillations.

## 1. Introduction and Motivation

Nonstandard neutrino interactions, parametrized by effective four-fermion operators of the form

$$\mathcal{L}_{NSI} = -2\sqrt{2}G_F \varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{fP}(\bar{\nu}_\alpha \gamma^\mu P_L \nu_\beta)(\bar{f}\gamma_\mu P f)$$

modify neutrino propagation through matter and can mimic or mask standard oscillation signals. As established in our previous study [Ref. 1], the Fermilab-to-Hyper-Kamiokande baseline (~1300 km) offers excellent sensitivity to the $\varepsilon_{e\tau}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mu\tau}$ parameters due to the large matter path length and high statistics achievable at a megaton-class water Cherenkov detector.

## 2. Theoretical Framework

The propagation Hamiltonian in matter is modified as:

$$H = \frac{1}{2E}\left[U \, \text{diag}(0, \Delta m^2_{21}, \Delta m^2_{31}) U^\dagger + A(x)\begin{pmatrix} 1+\varepsilon_{ee} & \varepsilon_{e\mu} & \varepsilon_{e\tau} \\ \varepsilon_{e\mu}^* & \varepsilon_{\mu\mu} & \varepsilon_{\mu\tau} \\ \varepsilon_{e\tau}^* & \varepsilon_{\mu\tau}^* & \varepsilon_{\tau\tau} \end{pmatrix}\right]$$

where $A(x) = 2\sqrt{2}G_F N_e(x) E$ encodes the matter potential. We adopt the same simulation framework as [Ref. 1], including realistic beam flux profiles, detector efficiencies, and systematic uncertainties appropriate for the Hyper-Kamiokande design report.

## 3. Sensitivity Projections

Using appearance and disappearance channels ($\nu_\mu \to \nu_e$, $\nu_\mu \to \nu_\mu$) with both neutrino and antineutrino running modes, we derive projected exclusion limits at 90% C.L.:

| Parameter | Current Bound | Projected FNAL-HK Sensitivity |
|-----------|---------------|-------------------------------|
| $|\varepsilon_{e\tau}|$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.3)$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.02)$ |
| $|\varepsilon_{\mu\tau}|$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.05)$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.01)$ |
| $|\varepsilon_{ee}-\varepsilon_{\mu\mu}|$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.4)$ | $\mathcal{O}(0.05)$ |

These improvements arise primarily from the extended baseline's enhanced matter effects combined with the substantial exposure (>$10$ MW-years) anticipated at Hyper-Kamiokande.

## 4. Implications for Topcolor Models

A particularly compelling application of these NSI constraints concerns topcolor-assisted technicolor (TC2) scenarios, wherein new strong dynamics generate the top quark mass while electroweak symmetry breaking proceeds via technicolor condensates. In such frameworks, the top-color interactions naturally induce flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNC) in the neutrino sector through:

- **Extended gauge boson exchange**: Heavy $Z'$ bosons associated with topcolor typically couple non-universally to third-generation fermions, generating tree-level $\varepsilon_{\mu\tau}$ and $\varepsilon_{e\tau}$ contributions when leptons mix with the third family.

- **Scale correlation**: The magnitude of induced NSI parameters scales as $\varepsilon \sim (g_{Z'}^2 v^2)/(M_{Z'}^2)$, directly linking neutrino oscillation sensitivity to the topcolor breaking scale, typically expected in the multi-TeV range.

Our projected sensitivity of $|\varepsilon_{\mu\tau}| \lesssim 0.01$ would translate into competitive bounds on $M_{Z'}/g_{Z'}$ ratios, complementary to collider searches at the LHC and future facilities. Specifically, for natural topcolor coupling strengths ($g_{Z'} \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$), this sensitivity probes $Z'$ masses up to several TeV—a range only partially accessible through direct production channels given projected luminosities.

## 5. Conclusions

The Fermilab-to-Hyper-Kamiokande configuration represents a powerful complementary probe of new physics in the neutrino sector, extending the reach established in [Ref. 1] to encompass constraints on topcolor-motivated flavor-violating interactions. These results underscore the value of long-baseline neutrino facilities not merely as precision tools for standard oscillation parameters, but as sensitive laboratories for physics beyond the electroweak scale, with particular relevance to dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking scenarios.

---
*This work extends the analysis framework of [Ref. 1], incorporating updated Hyper-Kamiokande design specifications and topcolor phenomenology relevant to current model-building efforts.*

# Abstract

We investigate the sensitivity of the proposed Hyper-Kamiokande experiment, using an upgraded NuMI-style neutrino beam, to nonstandard matter effects arising from new physics beyond the Standard Model. Building on previous studies that established the reach of long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments to generalized matter potentials, we extend the analysis to derive explicit constraints on the coupling constants and mediator masses of new light or intermediate-scale gauge bosons that could induce such effects. Nonstandard interactions (NSI) of neutrinos with matter, parametrized through effective four-fermion operators or new mediator exchange, modify the effective matter potential experienced by neutrinos as they propagate through the Earth, leading to observable deviations in oscillation probabilities at long baselines.

We perform a detailed simulation of the NuMI beam configuration as received at the Hyper-Kamiokande far detector, incorporating realistic beam flux, cross-section, and detector response, to assess the expected sensitivity to nonstandard matter potentials as a function of new physics parameters. By translating bounds on the effective NSI parameters $\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}$ into constraints on the underlying model parameters—namely the coupling strength $g'$ and the mass $M_{Z'}$ of a hypothetical new gauge boson—we map out the region of parameter space that can be probed by this long-baseline setup. We compare these projected bounds with existing constraints from neutrino scattering experiments, collider searches, and astrophysical observations, highlighting the complementary reach of oscillation experiments in probing light mediators with masses below a few GeV.

Our results demonstrate that the NuMI/Hyper-K configuration can achieve competitive or superior sensitivity to new physics scenarios in regions of parameter space relevant to solving the muon $g-2$ anomaly, dark matter portals, and other beyond-Standard-Model scenarios. We discuss the implications of these findings for future neutrino oscillation program design and highlight the value of long-baseline neutrino experiments as probes of physics beyond the Standard Model in the context of coupling-mass parameter space typically explored by dedicated fixed-target and collider searches.
